1.title: A Servant of God
1.context: The letter names its writer only as James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and its hearers as the twelve tribes of the Dispersion. The telling keeps to that self-description and builds no biography out of it; the book stands in the undated group, and the text gives no date for itself.
1.question: What does it mean to you that the writer introduces himself first as a servant, not by any office?

1.title: Consider It Pure Joy
1.context: Trials in this letter are not a detour from the faith but its testing ground. The word for testing here carries the picture of metal proved in fire, and perseverance is the product, not the mood, of the trial.
1.question: What trial in your life has changed you most, and can you see the perseverance it left behind?

1.title: Ask in Faith
1.context: Wisdom in James is not cleverness but the practical knowing that gets a person through trouble well. The promise is generous and without reproach, and the asking is asked to be steady, not wavering like a wave driven and tossed.
1.question: Where do you need wisdom right now, and what would asking without doubting look like this week?

1.title: The Rich Will Fade
1.context: The reversal runs both ways in one breath: the brother in humble circumstances exults in his high position, and the rich man in his low one, fading like a flower of the field under the scorching sun. The picture is drawn from the dry hills, where the flower is gone by afternoon.
1.question: Where do you measure your standing by wealth or by its lack, and what would James's reversal say to that?

1.title: The Crown of Life
1.context: The opening lesson closes where it began, with the man who perseveres under trial and the crown of life promised to those who love him. The crown here is the victor's wreath, not a king's gold, given at the end of the race, not the start.
1.question: What keeps you going under a trial that has not yet ended?

2.title: God Does Not Tempt
2.context: The first lesson ended with a crown for the man who perseveres; this one guards the source of the trial. Temptation's blame is shifted here away from God, who cannot be tempted by evil and tempts no one.
2.question: When you are tempted, where does your mind first put the blame?

2.title: Drawn Away by Desire
2.context: Temptation is traced to its own home: each person drawn away and enticed by his own desire, desire conceiving and giving birth to sin, sin grown up giving birth to death. The birth picture runs the whole chain from want to end in three steps.
2.question: What desire in your life is asking to be followed farther than it should go?

2.title: Every Good and Perfect Gift
2.context: Against the chain of desire the letter sets the opposite chain: every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow. The sun and moon shift and eclipse; the Giver does not.
2.question: What good gift in your life has come from a source you did not earn or control?

2.title: Firstfruits of His Creation
2.context: The unchanging God has already acted: he chose to give us birth through the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. Firstfruits are the first sheaf offered, the promise of the harvest still to come.
2.question: What does it mean to you that your new life is called a firstfruit, not the finished harvest?

3.title: Quick to Listen
3.context: The teaching turns from what God gives to how his people receive: quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger, because man's anger does not bring about the righteousness of God. The three speeds are given in one line, and the reason follows immediately.
3.question: Which of the three speeds is hardest for you: listening quickly, speaking slowly, or angering slowly?

3.title: Put Away the Filth
3.context: Before the word can be received it must have room: get rid of all moral filth and the evil that is so prevalent, and receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. The word is pictured as a seed already planted, waiting to be tended.
3.question: What needs clearing away before God's word can take root in you this week?

3.title: The Man in the Mirror
3.context: The blunt center of the chapter is a mirror: hearing without doing is like looking at your face and going away and immediately forgetting what you looked like. The mirror here is metal, dim, and unforgiving, and the forgetfulness is the point.
3.question: Where do you hear God's word clearly and still walk away unchanged?

3.title: The Perfect Law of Freedom
3.context: Against the forgetful hearer stands the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom and continues in it, not forgetful but effective, blessed in what he does. Law and freedom sit in one phrase here, not as opposites but as the same thing seen truly.
3.question: What would looking intently, rather than glancing, change in how you read Scripture?

3.title: Pure and Undefiled Religion
3.context: The chapter closes by testing religion at two points where it cannot be faked: the tongue held in check, and care for orphans and widows in their distress, kept unstained by the world. Two tests, one for speech and one for love, and both are named religion, not extras.
3.question: If your faith were tested at speech and at care for the vulnerable, where would it hold and where would it fail?

4.title: The Faith of Our Lord
4.context: Chapter 2 opens with a flat rule that sits on the whole section: as you hold out the faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism. The glory of the Lord is the reason given, not politeness or fairness in the abstract.
4.question: Where has favoritism crept into a place where faith should have ruled it out?

4.title: Suppose a Man Comes In
4.context: The illustration is introduced by James's own Suppose, and it is told as his supposition, not as an event that happened: a man in fine clothes and a gold ring, a poor man in shabby clothes, and the two seats they are given. The meeting place is the congregation's own gathering.
4.question: Have you ever watched the two seats get handed out, and which one were you given?

4.title: God Chose the Poor
4.context: The question the picture was built to force is asked in the open: has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him? The dishonor of the poor is then named, and the rich oppressors who drag hearers into court are named beside it.
4.question: What would it mean for a church to treat the poor as God treats them in this passage?

4.title: The Royal Law
4.context: His ground is the law itself: the royal law, Love your neighbor as yourself, quoted from Leviticus 19, and beside it the two commandments, Do not commit adultery and Do not murder. Favoritism is named as sin and lawbreaking, and breaking one point makes a person guilty of all.
4.question: Why does James treat favoritism as breaking the whole law, not as a small failure?

4.title: Mercy Triumphs Over Judgment
4.context: The section ends by aiming the whole thing at the hearers' own speech and action: speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law of freedom, for judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful, and mercy triumphs over judgment.
4.question: Where in your life is mercy being asked to triumph over the judgment you would rather give?

5.title: Go in Peace, Stay Warm
5.context: The claim his whole letter has been building toward is tested on a brother or sister without clothes and daily food, sent away with Go in peace; stay warm and well fed. Faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead, and the example is deliberately bare.
5.question: What good words have you given lately that should have come with food, clothing, or help?

5.title: Show Me Your Faith
5.context: James stages the argument the way a teacher stages an objection: someone will say, You have faith and I have deeds, and the answer is Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. The demons who believe and shudder are the proof that belief alone is not the line.
5.question: What deeds of yours show the faith you claim, and where is the gap?

5.title: Abraham Believed God
5.context: The evidence is Abraham offering Isaac, and the Genesis word carried whole: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness, and he was called God's friend. Faith working with action, and the Scripture fulfilled, are stated together, not apart.
5.question: How do you hold together believing God and acting on that belief, the way James holds them together here?

5.title: Rahab and the Spies
5.context: From Abraham he draws the conclusion in the open, a man justified by deeds and not by faith alone, and then the second witness: Rahab the prostitute, justified by her deeds when she received the messengers and sent them off by a different route. Two witnesses from opposite ends of Israel's story, one patriarch and one outsider.
5.question: What does it mean to you that James picks Rahab as his second witness, not another patriarch?

5.title: The Body Without the Spirit
5.context: The section ends with a body lying still: as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead. The comparison is short because it needs nothing added; the picture does all the work.
5.question: If your faith were a body, would it be breathing, and what would show it?

6.title: Not Many Teachers
6.context: Chapter 3 begins with a warning aimed at the people who teach, because teachers will be judged more strictly, and the reason is plain: we all stumble in many ways, and the person never at fault in what he says is able to keep his whole body in check.
6.question: Why does James warn teachers first, and what does that say about the power of words?

6.title: Bits and Rudders
6.context: The first two pictures are about control: bits in the mouths of horses turn the whole animal, and a small rudder turns a great ship driven by strong winds wherever the pilot wants to go. Small things steer large things, and the tongue is the small thing in the person.
6.question: What small thing steers your life more than it should, and who is holding it?

6.title: A Fire in the Forest
6.context: The third picture is not about control but about loss: how small a spark sets a great forest on fire, and the tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness, setting the whole course of life on fire, itself set on fire by hell. The hard saying stands at full strength, unsoftened.
6.question: What fire has a careless word started in your life, and what would putting it out take?

6.title: No Man Can Tame the Tongue
6.context: Man tames every kind of animal, bird, reptile, and sea creature, and has tamed them, but no man can tame the tongue: a restless evil, full of deadly poison. The claim is total, and it is the hinge of the chapter.
6.question: Where have you felt the tongue's untamability most, in your own speech or in someone else's?

6.title: Out of the Same Mouth
6.context: The proof offered is the double work every hearer knows: with the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men made in God's likeness, out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. Fresh water and salt water cannot flow from the same spring, nor a fig tree grow olives, and the question is left standing.
6.question: What does your tongue bless and curse in the same day, and what would consistency cost?

7.title: Who Is Wise?
7.context: After the tongue, James turns to the thing the tongue reveals: who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good life, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom. Wisdom here is proved by a life, not by a claim.
7.question: How would someone know you are wise without you telling them?

7.title: Bitter Jealousy
7.context: There is a counterfeit on the market, and James names its marks: bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart, boasting and denying the truth. The marks are inward first, and the boasting is the cover.
7.question: Where has jealousy or ambition dressed itself up as wisdom in your life?

7.title: Earthly, Unspiritual, Demonic
7.context: Then he gives the counterfeit its true name, all three at once: such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic, for where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice.
7.question: What disorder in a group you know traces back to jealousy or ambition?

7.title: Wisdom from Above
7.context: Against that portrait he sets the real thing, described in a string of marks: first of all pure, then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere. Eight marks, and the first one is purity.
7.question: Which mark of wisdom from above is most missing from your own decisions lately?

7.title: A Harvest of Righteousness
7.context: The chapter closes in a field: peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness. The harvest belongs to the sowing, and the sowing is peace itself, not a technique for getting peace later.
7.question: What peace could you sow this week, and what harvest might it reap?

8.title: What Causes Your Quarrels?
8.context: Chapter 4 opens by moving the battlefield inside: the conflicts and quarrels tearing the congregation come from the desires that battle within you, craving what you do not have, killing and coveting, fighting and quarreling, and not having because you do not ask.
8.question: What quarrel in your life is really a desire battling inside you?

8.title: You Ask Wrongly
8.context: Even the praying, when it happens, is bent by the same desires: you ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly, to spend what you get on your pleasures. Then the address turns sharp: You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?
8.question: Have you ever prayed for something and known, even as you prayed, that you wanted it for yourself?

8.title: God Opposes the Proud
8.context: James supports the charge with a Scripture line, and one seam shows on purpose: at 4:5 he writes the Scripture says for a line about the Spirit yearning with envy that matches no single older passage word for word, quoted here as James writes it, with no source address invented for it. Then the counterweight: God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble, from Proverbs 3.
8.question: What would it mean to receive grace as a humble person rather than to earn standing as a proud one?

8.title: Draw Near to God
8.context: The way out is a string of commands, and they come fast: submit yourselves to God, resist the devil and he will flee, draw near to God and he will draw near to you, wash your hands, purify your hearts, you double-minded. The promise inside the commands is that drawing near is answered.
8.question: Which command in this string is yours to obey first, and what is stopping you?

8.title: Humble Yourselves
8.context: The last commands go deeper than behavior, into feeling itself: grieve, mourn, and weep, turn laughter to mourning and joy to gloom, humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up. The lifting is his work, and it follows the humbling, not the other way around.
8.question: What would humbling yourself before the Lord look like in the situation you are facing now?

9.title: Do Not Slander
9.context: The chapter that began with wars inside the heart ends with the tongue again: brothers, do not slander one another, for anyone who speaks against a brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it, and if you judge the law you are not a practitioner of it but its judge.
9.question: Who have you judged lately in a way that put you above the law itself?

9.title: One Lawgiver and Judge
9.context: The seat he has taken is already occupied: there is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the one who is able to save and destroy, and the question lands on the hearer: but you, who are you to judge your neighbor?
9.question: What would change if you truly believed the judge's seat was already taken?

9.title: Today or Tomorrow
9.context: Then James turns and calls out a second group by their own words: Come now, you who say, Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business and make money. The plan is detailed, confident, and entirely his own.
9.question: What plan of yours is written as if tomorrow were already yours?

9.title: You Are a Mist
9.context: His answer is the picture this episode is named for: you do not even know what will happen tomorrow, what is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead, you ought to say, If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.
9.question: If your life is a mist, what would you spend today's brief appearance on?

9.title: Boasting in Proud Intentions
9.context: James closes the chapter by calling the old way what it is: as it is, you boast in your proud intentions, and all such boasting is evil, and anyone who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin. Knowing and doing are joined once more, as they have been all through the letter.
9.question: What right thing do you know to do that you have not yet done?

10.title: Weep and Wail
10.context: Chapter 5 opens with the same call James used on the planners: Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery that is coming upon you. The warning is addressed, direct, and unsoftened, and it is aimed at the rich as James has named them all through the letter.
10.question: How do you hear a warning that is addressed to the rich, and where do you stand in it?

10.title: Riches Have Rotted
10.context: He inventories their wealth, and every item in the inventory is already ruined: your riches have rotted, and moths have eaten your clothes. The wealth is described in the past tense, as if the ruin has already happened.
10.question: What wealth in your life is rotting even while you hold it?

10.title: Corroded Gold
10.context: Even the metals, the part of wealth that cannot rot, are gone: your gold and silver are corroded, their corrosion will testify against you and eat your flesh like fire, and you have hoarded wealth in the last days. The treasure kept for safety becomes the witness against its keeper.
10.question: What are you hoarding that might testify against you rather than for you?

10.title: The Wages You Withheld
10.context: Then James points at a sound: Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. The withheld wage is not silent, and its cry has an address.
10.question: Where has someone else's withheld pay, or your own, cried out, and who heard it?

10.title: Condemned the Righteous
10.context: The last two charges are the shortest and the heaviest: you have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence, you have fattened yourselves in the day of slaughter, you have condemned and murdered the righteous man, and he did not resist you. The righteous man's silence is the final indictment.
10.question: What does it mean that the righteous man James names did not resist, and what does that ask of you?

11.title: Patient Until the Lord's Coming
11.context: The verdict on the rich is read, and James turns to the hearers with the farmer's patience: be patient until the Lord's coming, see how the farmer waits for the land to yield its valuable crop, patiently waiting for the autumn and spring rains, strengthen your hearts, for the Lord's coming is near, and do not complain, for the Judge is standing at the door.
11.question: What are you waiting for, and what would farmer's patience look like while you wait?

11.title: The Prophets and Job
11.context: For examples of how to endure, James points backward, briefly, as is his way: the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as an example of patience in affliction, blessed are those who have persevered, you have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen what the Lord finally brought about, the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. Job's perseverance and the outcome from the Lord are stated as James states them, with no explanation attached that he does not give. Then the rule about oaths, above all, do not swear, so that you will not fall under judgment.
11.question: What has endurance taught you that comfort never could?

11.title: Prayer, Songs, and Oil
11.context: Then the letter's last movement gathers up the community's whole life: is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing songs of praise. Is anyone sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer offered in faith will restore the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has sinned, he will be forgiven. The prayer and healing words are carried exactly as written, with no added medical verdict in either direction.
11.question: Which of the three, prayer, song, or the elders' prayer, is yours to reach for today?

11.title: The Prayer of a Righteous Man
11.context: From the elders' prayer James widens the practice to everyone: confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed, for the prayer of a righteous man is powerful and effective. Elijah, a man just like us, prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years, and again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain and the earth produced its crops. Elijah's story stays in James's compression, not re-expanded here.
11.question: What prayer of yours has been powerful and effective, and what made it so?

11.title: Turning a Wanderer Back
11.context: The letter has no farewell. Its last words are about one person: my brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, remember this: whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save him from death and cover over a multitude of sins. The book ends on a rescue, not a goodbye.
11.question: Who in your life has wandered, and what would bringing them back look like, gently?
